details:
**Kata Tjuta (the Olgas)**
A group of 36 domed rock formations about 25 km west of Uluru, formerly called the Olgas. The two landmarks share Uluru–Kata Tjuta National Park, and they are thought to connect beneath the surrounding sand.

**Anangu people**
The Aboriginal traditional owners of Uluru, many of whom speak the Pitjantjatjara language. They ask visitors not to photograph certain sacred parts of the rock, such as sections of its northeast face.

**Alice Springs**
The town in the center of the Northern Territory that is the usual gateway for visitors, about 450 km by road northeast of Uluru. Many tourists also fly into Ayers Rock Airport near the resort town of Yulara.

**Northern Territory**
The Australian territory where Uluru lies, in its southwest corner. The territory also contains the MacDonnell Ranges.

**Red sandstone monolith**
Uluru is a huge red rock formation made of arkose, a coarse sandstone rich in feldspar, which has a grain similar to granite. It rises about 348 m above the surrounding desert, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

**1985 handback**
In 1985 the Australian government under Prime Minister Bob Hawke returned ownership of Uluru and the park to the Anangu, who leased it back to the national parks service. The campaign for the handback was led by the Central Land Council.

**William Gosse and the name Ayers Rock**
In 1873 the surveyor William Gosse became the first European to see the rock. He named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, then Chief Secretary of South Australia.

**Ernest Giles**
An explorer who traveled through the area in 1872 and saw Kata Tjuta, and who also found the nearby Finke River and Lake Amadeus. He was overshadowed by Gosse, who reached Uluru itself the next year.

**Dual naming in 1993**
In 1993 the landmark was officially given the dual name "Ayers Rock / Uluru," which was reversed to "Uluru / Ayers Rock" in 2002.

**Tjukurpa (the Dreamtime)**
The Anangu belief system and law, which describes how ancestral beings created the land, including Uluru. Songlines and stories such as that of Kalaya the emu are tied to the rock.

**Mutitjulu Waterhole**
A permanent waterhole at the base of Uluru, sacred to the Anangu. The nearby Aboriginal community of Mutitjulu is named after it.

**Azaria Chamberlain**
A nine-week-old baby who disappeared from a campsite near Uluru in 1980. Her mother Lindy claimed a dingo took her, and was wrongly convicted of murder before being exonerated. The phrase "a dingo ate my baby" was later parodied on Seinfeld.

**Climbing ban and Pauline Hanson**
Climbing Uluru, long discouraged by the Anangu, was banned in October 2019. In 2019, before the ban took effect, the right-wing politician Pauline Hanson attempted the climb for a TV segment in protest and got stuck partway up.

**Petermann Orogeny**
A mountain-building event in central Australia over 500 million years ago that formed the ancient mountains whose eroded sediments became the rock of Uluru and Kata Tjuta.

**Mount Conner**
A flat-topped mesa east of Uluru, often mistaken for it by travelers. Along with Uluru and Kata Tjuta, it is one of the three great rock formations of the region.
